newsitem.title: USA: U.S. budget talks reopen with "solid" meeting.
newsitem.headline: U.S. budget talks reopen with "solid" meeting.

text.p: The White House and Congress reopened stalled budget negotiations Tuesday with Republican leaders vowing to go ahead with their own plan if compromises on spending and taxes are not reached soon.
President Bill Clinton urged his negotiators to remain flexible on the numerous thorny issues from taxes to health-care spending as the sessions got underway in a basement room of the Capitol.
The negotiators emerged after a 3-1/2 hour meeting agreeing to meet again but far from ready to shake hands on a deal to balance the budget in five years.

Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, called it "a solid meeting." Earlier he had said the decision to meet marked the beginning of a new phase in this year's budget negotiations.
The talks will resume Wednesday and are expected to go through the week, but Republicans warned they expected significant progress soon.
"Today was just a start. Clearly over the next few days we will see just how far the president and his negotiators will be willing to go," Domenici said.

House Budget Committee chairman John Kasich, Republican of Ohio, said he has been preparing an alternative budget proposal and will seek out allies among conservative Democrats, if no compromise is reached with the White House.
"We are kind of at the end of the road. We are either going to see some progress made over the course of the week or we are not going to reach any agreement in the short term," Kasich said.

His Democratic counterpart on the House Budget Committee cautioned against reading too much into the meeting. "We are a long, long way off. We shouldn't raise false expectations today," Representative John Spratt, Democrat of South Carolina, said.
The bargaining opened at 1 p.m. EDT with a discussion of ways to control the growth of spending on Medicare, the programme that serves 63 million elderly and disabled persons.
Clinton's chief budget negotiator Frank Raines said the administration would stand by its pledge to curb Medicare growth by $100 billion over the next five years.
Congressional analysts have said the president's plan saves only $81.6 billion in Medicare over that time frame. Most of the savings come from payments to health care providers.

Raines said the meeting "kicked off a good session" and he reiterated the president's commitment to balance the budget by 2002. He hoped this series of meetings would be the "culmination" of the budget negotiations.
His team included White House Economic Policy Council chief Gene Sperling, Health and Human Services Secretary Donna Shalala and White House congressional liaison John Hilley.
Disputes between the White House and the Republicans in the last Congress led to Clinton's veto of spending bills and two partial government shutdowns.
Before the budget session, Republican leaders emerged from a private meeting with statements that they remained committed to substantial tax cuts for families and investors.
